chunks: And what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn Mūsā al-Khashshāb, from Ghiyāth ibn Kallūb, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Jaʿfar, from his father عليه السلام: that ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn عليه السلام instructed that an umm walad of his should perform ghusl for him when he died, so she performed ghusl for him.

Because the proper way regarding these two reports is that we restrict them specifically to those two عليهم السلام. And the basis for that is what the first report contains: that there was no one there who was permitted to directly handle Fāṭimah and Maryam عليهما السلام. And likewise is the statement regarding the second report; otherwise, the fundamental principle is what we have mentioned.

key_terms.أُمُّ وَلَدٍ: a slave-mother who bore a child for her master
key_terms.الْأَصْلُ: the foundational rule or default legal principle
key_terms.الْخَبَرَيْنِ: the two reports being discussed and interpreted together
key_terms.الْوَجْهُ: the proper interpretive basis or juristic explanation
key_terms.نَقْصُرَهُمَا: to restrict their application to a specific case
key_terms.يُبَاشِرَ: to directly handle or attend physically in the context of washing the deceased

ai.seo_question: How do Shia scholars reconcile reports about exceptional cases of post-death ghusl between spouses or specific holy figures?
ai.summary: This passage discusses a legal ruling concerning whether a man may perform ghusl for his wife and a woman for her husband after death. It presents a report with its sanad and then explains that certain exceptional reports are to be restricted specifically to particular cases involving the Maʿṣūmīn عليهم السلام, while the general legal principle remains as previously stated.
